flags.title: A sibling repository's Bour & Davy consistency test inserts the cumulative exponent where the published relation needs the density exponent
flags.evidence: Bour & Davy (1999, GRL 26(13) 2001-2004, abstract read at Wiley 2026-10-02): x = (a - 1)/D, where a is the exponent of the frequency-length distribution and x the exponent of the mean distance to the nearest larger neighbour. GEMSDOE22 scripts/02_fit_clustering.py fits N(>=L) = C L^-a (a CUMULATIVE exponent, e.g. its alpha_ols 2.02) and then evaluates (a - 1)/D with it; its reported 'D_consistent: true' therefore does not test the published relation. Here the relation was checked by simulation: 6,000-point populations with Levy-dust positions of dimension D and Pareto lengths of density exponent a, five (a, D) settings x 3 seeds - the measured x is bracketed by the geometric-mean and arithmetic-mean estimators around (a - 1)/D and is far from (a - 2)/D (tests/test_faultstats.py). On the real catalogue: a = 3.15 [2.99, 3.34] above 2.95 km, D = 1.51-1.66, predicted x in [1.20, 1.55], measured tail x = 1.54 [1.33, 1.75] (centroid distance) and 1.84 [1.57, 2.13] (edge distance): consistent for the centroid definition, marginal for the edge definition; over all lengths x = 0.92. Caveat: the paper body could not be read (the Wiley e-PDF viewer is blocked), so the density reading is derived (N(>l) ~ l^-(a-1), nearest of N(>l) fractal points at d ~ N^(-1/D)) and confirmed numerically, not read from the text.
flags.action: src/gems/faultstats.py defines a as the density exponent everywhere and reports the cumulative form (a - 1) alongside; the simulation is a unit test. The sibling's number is not reused.
flags.how_established: read at source (abstract) + measured here (docs/data/fault-statistics.json, tests/test_faultstats.py)

flags.title: H24's 100,000 dots carry a spectral line at exactly the GeoDAWN Area 2 flight-line spacing
flags.evidence: Verified survey geometry (USGS GeoDAWN metadata, mirrored): traverse lines every 400 m (east-west), tie lines every 4,000 m; Area 1 200 m / 2,000 m; Area 1 is 4.7 % of the footprint. The detector (peak power at the survey period over the median of the surrounding band, ranked against 60 control frequencies) finds the 400 m line in the official tmi_hg band (strength 86.9 vs control 95th percentile 6.6) and the 4 km tie-line period in tmi, rtp and tmi_vg, so the survey is visible in the 100 m inputs. H24's dots: strength 243.3 vs control p95 10.0, rank p = 0.016 (the minimum attainable); rows by phase mod 4 = [0.223, 0.235, 0.307, 0.235]. Cause only partly attributed: non-maximum suppression on a RANDOM score produces no line (strength 6.3, p = 0.10) and rank noise of sigma = 0.1 removes it, so the comb is in the score S; the vote map V carries a weak one through ens12-adopted (28.7, p = 0.016) but dropping that voter does not clear the emission, none of the eight habitat layers has a significant line, and the phase of the emission comb (3.1 rad) lies between that of tmi_hg (2.9) and that of S/V/H/ens12 (-2.2 = 4.1), so inheritance from the survey cannot be separated from a coincidence. Across the 23 live-scored emissions the line strength does not correlate with the live score (Spearman -0.15, p = 0.50, n = 23): there is no evidence that the comb hurts the score; it is flagged as an artefact risk for the Phase 2 reviewers.
flags.action: scripts/build_audited_emission.py equalises the row phases inside 30 km blocks, moving only the excess dots by 1-2 px (H29 5.4%, H30 2.1%; mean shift 1.45/1.56 px). Re-audit: strength 2.4 (p = 0.74) / 2.3 (p = 0.84); K-bar, eta and coverage are unchanged to four decimals for H29.
flags.how_established: measured here (docs/data/prediction-audit.json, h29-build.json, h30-build.json); geometry read from the USGS GeoDAWN metadata file

flags.title: The Hermant et al. (2025) '~400 m misregistration' was stated more strongly than the source
flags.evidence: Figure 2 caption of the paper (read at pangea.stanford.edu 2026-10-02): 'Local discrepancy observed in North Central Nevada: distance between USGS Quaternary faults and TLS fault label can be up to 400m.'
